Let me analyze this conflict.

Axis: applicant
- Register: "Franklin Fueling Systems / Intelligent Controls Inc"
- Document: "Franklin Fueling Systems"

The register value contains two names joined with "/": "Franklin Fueling Systems / Intelligent Controls Inc". The document context from the certificate's own text (the extraction comments, which appear to be metadata embedded in the extracted text) shows: "<!-- applicant: Franklin Fueling Systems / Intelligent Controls Inc -->". Interesting — the embedded metadata in the document says "Franklin Fueling Systems / Intelligent Controls Inc", which matches the register.

But the conflict presented says document: "Franklin Fueling Systems". This likely comes from the visible text of the certificate (the actual applicant line in the certificate body), which presumably says "Franklin Fueling Systems" only, while the register says both names.

So which is right? The document is the legal instrument. If the certificate document itself lists the applicant as "Franklin Fueling Systems" only, while the register lists "Franklin Fueling Systems / Intelligent Controls Inc"...

Hmm, but wait — the embedded comments in the document context show applicant: "Franklin Fueling Systems / Intelligent Controls Inc". These comments appear to be provenance metadata from the extraction pipeline (extraction_method: glm-ocr, source_pdf, cert_id matching register id 3311). These are essentially the register's data embedded as comments, not the certificate's actual content. So the "document" value "Franklin Fueling Systems" comes from the certificate's visible text.

Is "Franklin Fueling Systems" vs "Franklin Fueling Systems / Intelligent Controls Inc" a same-entity case? Franklin Fueling Systems and Intelligent Controls Inc — Intelligent Acquisition... Actually, Intelligent Controls Inc is a related company (Franklin Fueling Systems was formerly known as... actually FE Petro and INCON are brands of Franklin Fueling Systems; Intelligent Controls, Inc. (INCON) is part of Franklin Fueling Systems). But per the rules: "Genuinely different company or person names = different-entity (best_value = the document's, since the certificate is the legal instrument)."

Here it's not that one is a misspelling of the other; the register includes an additional entity. The document names only "Franklin Fueling Systems". Is that "different-entity"? The names aren't spelling drift — the register's value includes an extra company. The document value is a subset. The legal instrument (certificate) says the applicant is Franklin Fueling Systems. The register says both. Per rules, when genuinely different (not same after normalization), best_value = document's.

Alternatively, could argue "same-entity" since Franklin Fueling Systems appears in both — the register's value is a superset. The conflict resolution rule for same-entity cases: spelling drift, legal-suffix drift, accent differences = same-entity, and presumably best_value is register canonical. But this isn't spelling drift; it's an additional entity in the register. The rules say genuinely different company names = different-entity, best = document.

I think the intended answer: "different-entity" with best_value = "Franklin Fueling Systems" because the certificate document itself (the legal instrument) names only Franklin Fueling Systems as applicant, while the register adds Intelligent Controls Inc — an entity not attested in the certificate text.

But wait — consider: could "Franklin Fueling Systems" in the doc vs the register's combined name be considered same-entity with the register carrying the fuller canonical form? The rules mention "Number/year format differences that clearly denote the same certificate = same-entity with the register's canonical form" — that's for certificate numbers. For names, same-entity is for spelling/suffix/accent drift. Adding "/ Intelligent Controls Inc" is not drift; it's a genuinely different (additional) name. So different-entity, best_value from document = "Franklin Fueling Systems".

One short sentence for why: The certificate (legal instrument) names only Franklin Fueling Systems; Intelligent Controls Inc appears only in the register entry, so the fused record should carry the document's applicant.
